content: Orange oil is an essential oil derived from the glands located within the peel of an orange fruit. It is typically obtained through extraction or steam distillation as a by-product of orange juice production. The primary component of orange oil is d-limonene, which is often used as a substitute for pure lemon oil. Pure lemon oil can be further isolated from orange oil through distillation. Limonene Limonene is the compound responsible for the characteristic aroma of citrus fruits. Due to its pleasant fragrance, it is widely utilized in the production of perfumes and household cleaning products. Additionally, limonene functions as an effective, environmentally friendly, and relatively safe solvent. This makes it a preferred active ingredient in various applications, including adhesive removers, stain removers, general-purpose cleaners, and paint strippers. Safety The d-limonene found in orange oil acts as a mild skin irritant because it dissolves the protective oils present on the skin. For this reason, it is advisable to wear solvent-resistant gloves when handling solutions containing limonene. Furthermore, limonene is combustible. For example, squeezing an orange peel near an open flame can cause the oil glands to release an aerosol that ignites upon contact with the flame. In toxicological studies, limonene has been observed to induce cancer in male rats by interacting with α2U-globulin, a protein not produced by female rats. However, there is no evidence to suggest that limonene is carcinogenic or genotoxic in humans. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies d-limonene as a Group 3 substance, meaning it is not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans. For further information on its regulatory status and toxicity, refer to detailed studies on limonene. Insecticide d-Limonene serves as a natural insect repellent for citrus fruits. When insects come into direct contact with d-limonene, it acts as an organic insecticide. However, experiments with fruit flies have demonstrated that they circumvent this defense mechanism by laying their eggs in areas between the oil-producing glands of the fruit.
